claim.description: A proposition, including proposals, user-stated positions and challenged formulations; status records its standing.

question.description: An unresolved or answered inquiry; answers are linked claims.

case.description: An experience or case-study summary, with source provenance.

source.description: A source artifact or provenance context.

entity.description: A named domain role or object type that statements refer to; subtype is recorded in metadata.

operation.description: A named action whose meaning is distinct from its permission or implementation.

trace.description: An explicitly bounded event trace extracted from evidence or constructed as a synthetic fixture. Roles are recorded at event time.

check-result.description: A reproducible bounded pattern evaluation tied to exact claim and trace inputs; not a proof of the prose theory.

supports.description: Source supplies a reason to believe the target claim; not a proof.

answers.description: Claim offers full, partial or unknown coverage of a question. Only a current accepted full answer resolves it; partial answers preserve the remainder.

challenges.description: Source disputes or supplies a potential counterexample to the target claim.

revises.description: Source updates or corrects the target earlier formulation.

motivates.description: Source explains why the target question is worth asking; does not answer it.

informs.description: Source contributes context for the target proposal without logical entailment.

raises.description: Source gives rise to the target unresolved question.

about.description: Source claim, question or evidence concerns the target domain anchor; no assertion of truth or implication.

governs.description: Source claim specifies a responsibility, permission or constraint concerning the target operation; conditions remain in the claim text.

potential-conflict.description: Recorded possible incompatibility between claims requiring interpretation of conditions and scope. Not proof of contradiction.

checks.description: A saved computation checked this input; does not imply support or acceptance.

depends-on.description: Dependent question or claim → mandatory prerequisite. The dependent is not ready until the prerequisite is answered or accepted. Use only for a real dependency.

acts-on.description: Operation → the entity it reads or changes. Lets a reader walk from an entity to the operations on it.

extracted-from.description: Interpretation was extracted from the source. Source fingerprints bind saved evidence; the source needs no accepted standing.

performed-by.description: Operation → the role that performs it. Lets a reader walk from a role to what it does.

agent-definition.text: Candidate: A = (R, C, U, J), accompanied by a running policy P = (start, drive). This separates what an agent owes, what it reads, what it can do and how it judges, from what launches it and permits its next turn. This is a candidate construction, not a ratified definition.

session-2026-09-16-record-creation.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "the steward is always the one that creates a record. Every single record creation has to go through the steward." "we want a centralized, singular location for record creation, and that is the steward." "the observation-to-task materialization system is plugging a hole that exists, which the steward is going to fill properly." "the steward is responsible for inter-store communication and managing, basically." On team nodes: "the record is in the normal outer graph, and the sub-items are really just attributes of that record itself. ... I wouldn't even call it creation, because creation means that something new is written." On thresholds: "I would rather the orchestrator just use its own intelligence to bring that to my attention." "the orchestrator will decide, 'Okay, I'm probably going to ask the operator if we should give this back to the steward, and I'll pass on the notes about what went wrong, and then the steward decides.'"

steward-creates-every-record.text: Every record creation goes through the steward. The steward is the single place where records are created, so a record whose premise or approach is wrong is caught where it is chosen rather than wedging in the graph.

meta.title: Only the steward creates records
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: Settled 2026-09-16; exact words in session-2026-09-16-record-creation.

steward-owns-inter-store.text: The steward is responsible for communication between stores: turning a record in one store into a record in another (an observation into a task, a passed design review into observations). The live contract's materialization adapter and review-spawned observations are stopgaps that the steward will replace; this was never the orchestrator's job.

meta.title: The steward owns inter-store creation
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: Settled 2026-09-16 when the obs_to_task adapter and spawned_observation_ids in contracts/internal/morphisms/contract.mor were raised as edge cases.

team-line-items-are-attributes.text: Team-node line items are not record creation. The record stays in the outer graph; its line-items array is fragmented into items by the kernel, system-owned, and run through the team system. Nothing new is written as a record, so the steward rule is not involved.

meta.title: Team line items are attributes, not records
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: Settled 2026-09-16 when D310 team nodes were raised as an edge case.

orchestrator-judges-then-asks.text: There is no configured failure threshold. The orchestrator uses its own judgment to notice that an attempt is going wrong and brings it to the operator: it asks whether to keep trying or hand the record back to the steward, passing on notes about what went wrong. The steward then decides.

meta.title: No threshold: the orchestrator judges, then asks
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: 2026-09-16. Rejects the configurable N-failures idea that the earlier claim's 'stopping threshold' wording assumed. The ask-the-operator-first substance of that claim stands.

session-2026-09-16-rest.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "The terminal node in one of the dimensions of a store does not necessarily always mean that the work was completed successfully. ... it means that the movement of this record through this dimension has come to rest." "what completed means is that there is no more movement of this thing through that dimension." "the steward should be woken if the record has completed, or in this case, if the record has been abandoned. I don't know what our schema choice is here; this is an open question." "the steward waking conditions are on a new intention that has been filed and not processed." "The operator will not be the handover mechanism from the orchestrator to the steward. Instead, there should be some kind of artifact or reference note, probably written by the orchestrator, that will explain what went wrong, why, and what the orchestrator's recommendation is. Ultimately, it's up to the steward what to do." "Maybe the archive has a note, and that note is the handover from orchestrator to steward."

terminal-means-rest.text: A terminal state in a dimension means the record's movement through that dimension has come to rest, not that the work succeeded. An investigation that finds no problem ends at rest. A record archived before reaching a terminal state has also come to rest.

meta.title: Terminal means rest, not success
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: A standing Morphisms philosophy restated 2026-09-16; exact words in session-2026-09-16-rest.

rest-wakes-steward.text: The steward becomes claimable for an intention when any linked record comes to rest, whether completed or abandoned, and when a new intention has been filed and not yet processed. This generalizes the earlier completion-only rule; the extra computation stays an accepted cost.

meta.title: Rest wakes the steward
meta.author: Blake
meta.provenance: 2026-09-16; generalizes completion-wakes-steward using terminal-means-rest.

orchestrator-handover-artifact.text: The operator is not the handover channel from orchestrator to steward. When an attempt is given back, the orchestrator writes a durable handover: what went wrong, why, and its recommendation, with references to the events, plans and linked records it saw. The steward reads it and decides what to do next.

archive-reason-is-handover.text: The handover from orchestrator to steward is the reason recorded on the record's archive event. session-2026-09-16-dials.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "there are dials which are extremely useful. They basically are my weights across different axes that are configurable by the user in terms of what should come to my desk and what the steward can automatically handle." "I can change the number of dials, the wording of the dial, and the weight from 0 to 10." "Not everything has to go through my desk." "as long as there is a trace about why it came to me, then I can control it, right? You can only improve things that you can measure." "the fact that it came to me is perfect because now it tells me how the steward reads it and interprets my meaning, my words. Then I can change the configuration." "I don't want the graph to contain highly specific things unless they provide extremely useful case studies."

operator-role.text: The human who owns the product and settles what the steward sends up. A formal actor like the agent roles, not a channel. Blake today.

dials-configure-steward.text: The steward's autonomy is bounded by dials: operator-authored sentences, each with a weight from 0 to 10, saying what should reach the operator and what the steward may handle itself. The steward weighs an intention against them and either files work directly or sends the intention to the operator. The set of dials is open; the operator adds, rewords and reweights them.

file-intention.text: Bring a new intention into existence. The front door: anyone outside, or any agent, may file. Filing wakes nobody; the intention is ready or waiting by its kind (claimability-not-waking).

reassess-intention.text: The steward claims an intention and reads all prior work against it, then chooses: more work, wait, send to the desk, or settle. Triggered by rest of a linked record or a new filing.

send-to-desk.text: Put an item on the operator's desk with a trace of why. Not steward-only: the steward sends intentions the dials say the operator must see; the orchestrator sends execution questions directly. While the item is on the desk the operator owes the next action.

answer-at-desk.text: The operator answers an item on the desk, at the desk or in an agent thread. The answer is recorded against the durable item and ownership of the next action returns to the sender.

settle-intention.text: Judge an intention satisfied or withdrawn. Performed by the steward or the operator, never by a record completing.

intention-operation-set.text: The operations on an intention are: file (anyone), claim and reassess (steward), create a linked record (steward only), send to the desk (steward for intentions, orchestrator for execution questions), answer at the desk (operator), settle (steward or operator). No operation on an intention belongs to the orchestrator or a worker except the orchestrator's direct desk question.

desk-item.text: An item on the operator's desk: a question, a proposal with options, or a block the orchestrator or steward cannot settle, or a record resting at an operator seat projected by the kernel. Linked to the intention(s) it concerns and to zero or more records across them; an intention sent up by the steward has no record yet, an obstruction may span many. Carries its own dated log (the discussion and the operator's answers). Answered once, then closed.

run.text: One worker's turn on a record at a node: the pair (record, worker). Started by the orchestrator, claimed by the worker. Its events are a span of the record's log. Rest of a run wakes the orchestrator.

one-actor-one-item-kind.text: Each actor claims exactly one kind of item and no other: the steward claims intentions, the orchestrator claims runs, the worker claims records, the operator claims desk items. session-2026-09-16-ladder.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "there is this relation which is essentially all about trying to get an intention realised. at each stage something can obstruct this process." "perhaps it's better to think about obstructions to the claimee? steward obs -> desk (resolver=operator) ... worker obs -> flag (resolver=contract auditor)" "Of course this needs to be finite, otherwise we regress." "two types of edges: births/is an attempt at, versus blocked." "i like the idea of the operator being the terminal; makes sense." So do we have many intentions linked to one desk item?" On delegates: "yes, that's pretty good."

worker-role.text: The agent role that performs one run: a contract-governed turn on a record at a node. Constrained by packet, schema and legal edges.

auditor-role.text: The agent role that resolves flags: it rules on whether and how the contract should change. Acts on the frame, not the ladder.

flag.text: A marker that the contract blocked a run: the worker could not do the work as the contract stands. Resolver: the auditor. Never about the record, the worker, tooling or environment (session 1 F3).

contract.text: The frame an attempt runs under: stores, dimensions, states, edges, schemas, personas. Not a rung on the ladder; changing it is not an attempt at an intention.

start-run.text: The orchestrator starts a worker on a record at a node. Births a run.

return-run.text: The worker ends its run with an outcome: done, or blocked with reason and evidence. Rest of a run wakes the orchestrator.

raise-obstruction.text: A blocked actor raises an obstruction off the ladder: a desk item (resolver operator) for what the orchestrator or steward cannot settle, or a flag (resolver auditor) only when the contract blocks the run. It names the rungs it is about and which of them it holds while it is open.

rule-on-flag.text: The auditor resolves a flag: rules whether the contract changes. The change itself is frame work by the contract writer, not a record.

operator-is-terminal-resolver.text: Every obstruction has a resolver, and every resolver chain ends at the operator: worker to orchestrator, orchestrator and steward to the operator, worker-about-the-contract to the auditor, auditor to the operator. The operator is the only actor with no resolver. This is what makes the obstruction structure finite.

flag-is-an-obstruction.text: A flag is the representation of an obstruction that arose during the attempted manifestation of an intention, and says the contract is the problem. Its resolver is the auditor.

contract-changes-are-not-records.text: Contract improvements are not records and are not treated as attempts at an intention. They are changes to the frame, made by the contract writer under the operator or after an auditor ruling.

everything-enters-as-intention.text: The user story is one sentence: add it to Morphisms. Whatever enters (a bug, a question, a feature, an idea, a PR) enters as an intention. Records, runs, desk items and flags are all derived from intentions.

obstruction-links-many-rungs.text: An obstruction is off the ladder and points at whatever it stopped: one or many records, across one or many intentions. Its fields are who raised it, who resolves it, which rungs it is about, and which of those it holds while it is open. These are fields, not kinds.

attempt-ladder.text: One relation, 'is one attempt at', repeated: a record is one attempt at an intention; a run is one attempt at a record's node. Claimed by steward, orchestrator, worker respectively. When a rung comes to rest, the rung above becomes claimable again: run rest makes the record claimable by the orchestrator, record rest makes the intention ready for the steward.

meta.title: attempt ladder
meta.author: assistant

attempt-obstruction-dual.text: On the ladder, two shapes cover what happens to an intention: it moves (an attempt: record, run) or it is blocked (an obstruction). Attempts go down the ladder, are born from the claimer above, are claimed by a doer, rest when the walk ends, and make the rung above claimable again. A block goes sideways to a resolver and holds the rungs it names: a flag when the contract is the cause (resolver auditor), otherwise up to the orchestrator and, if it cannot settle it, to the desk; resolution makes the held rung claimable again. The desk itself is not an obstruction shape: it also receives non-blocking questions, dials-routed intentions and records resting at an operator seat. An agent-filed intention is neither: it is a new intention entering the front door.

contract-is-the-frame.text: The contract is the frame the ladder runs under, not a rung. A flag is the one place the ladder points at the frame. Blake: 'getting better, hasn't fully clicked'.

delegates-are-co-seats.text: The assistant and the architect are not actors. They are the operator with a co-seat on one of the operator's own items: the assistant on a desk item for hours, the architect on an intention the operator has taken (the dials route architecture decisions to the desk) for weeks. A design session is the operator stewarding one intention with a co-seat; the theory graph is that seat's ledger. Any user-defined agent has three coordinates: which operator item it shares, how it is driven, how long it lives. Blake: 'yes, that's pretty good'.

abandonment-is-archive.text: An abandoned record is archived outside its dimensions, not walked to a terminal state inside one. The archive event carries the handover reason; rest, not success, is what the steward sees.

intention-history-reuses-record-events.text: An intention's history uses the kernel's append-only event machinery, the same mechanism records use, though an intention is not a record. No overwritten fields; each actor's actions on an item append to that item's log.

one-log-per-item-kind.text: Each item kind has its own append-only log, written by the actions of whoever claims it: worker and orchestrator actions append to the record log (a run is a span of it, not a log of its own), steward actions to the intention log, operator actions to the desk item log. Other agents extend the same pattern.

observation-is-a-typed-intention.text: An observation is a machine-readable type of intention, filed by the worker at the front door with a signature: which worker filed it and what kind it is. It is one of the steward's inboxes, not a separate object and not on the ladder. For now the friction envelope stays for Morphisms' own dogfood.

worker-inbox-under-user-dials.text: The steward processes the agent-filed inbox at volume only when the user turns it on: recency dials bound how far back it reads, a cost estimate from historical data is shown before it runs, and the user picks the model. Off by default; an old backlog is never replayed whole.

process-worker-inbox.text: The steward reads agent-filed intentions within the user's recency window, discards or merges the noise, and reassesses the rest. Turned on by the user; costed before it runs.

sorter-is-not-an-actor.text: There is no sorter actor. Filtering worker-filed intentions is the steward working one of its inboxes; the required actors stay three.

session-2026-09-16-discussion.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim: "Discussions are merely event logs for desk items. That's my proposal. Yeah, that's my proposal. They are dated. I think they would honestly just be... maybe they have a schema, you know? Maybe. I don't know. That should probably be configurable. But basically, the agent that I'm working with will fill in the discussion, and again, the discussion is dated." "These are the work logs that I've been running manually, using a new note in my work logs. Then I have to keep going back and finding them ... This should be tracked more explicitly, and we might even link in the future. ... This theory-graph system is actually working very well. But anyway, that would be more like an extension or an add-on."

discussion-is-desk-item-log.text: A discussion is the desk item's own event log: dated entries appended by the operator or by the co-seat agent working with the operator. It replaces the hand-written worklog notes. Entry shape is configurable; a theory graph may link in later as an extension.

intention-schema-draft.text: Schema of an intention. Identity and filing: id, the filed text, filed_by, kind (filing origin: person-filed or agent-filed, derived from the session with an explicit override; subject is never a field). One state: ready, waiting, settled; settled is rest and final, with satisfied or withdrawn on the settle event; the steward's claim is the pen, not a state. History: one append-only event log on the kernel's record-event machinery, events for filed, reassessed (choice and reason as payload), record linked, record rest, sent to desk (trace as payload), desk answered, settled (outcome as payload); each dated with actor. Links: the records that are attempts at it; the desk items it birthed, each carrying its own log. No artifacts and no discussion of its own. Not a record.

intention-kind-registry.text: Is an intention's kind a fixed set shipped with Morphisms, a user-configurable registry, or free text with a few reserved values (such as observation)?

reassessment-reasoning-location.text: Where does the steward's reasoning at reassessment live: as the payload of the reassessed event on the intention log, or somewhere else? The dials trace already lives on the send-to-desk event.

intention-has-no-artifacts.text: Does an intention carry no artifacts at all, with everything durable living in its event log and its desk items' logs? Blake is wary of artifacts on intentions; the draft assumes none.

session-2026-09-16-kind-artifacts.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim, on kind: "if they modify the types, then they need an agent that will consume those types ... if there is no agent set to process those kinds, that's user error, and we would show that as an alert. I don't know how much freedom we give. Maybe we start with a fixed set until we prove that we need more ... Yeah, let's go with that. Less is more." On attention state: "Does the steward's attention really need to be separate from the base state? Can't we collapse it down?" On artifacts: "Maybe less is more, I think. My original idea was, can we think of intentions as just another type of record? But we don't need that, I think, do we?"

intention-kind-fixed-set.text: An intention's kind comes from a fixed set shipped with Morphisms, not a user registry, until a real need proves otherwise. Reason: a user-added kind needs an agent configured to consume it, and an unconsumed kind is a user error the system would have to alert on.

intention-carries-no-artifacts.text: An intention carries no artifacts. Everything durable about it is in its event log and in its desk items' logs.

intention-single-state.text: An intention has one state, not two: ready, claimed, waiting, satisfied, withdrawn. Open is just 'not yet satisfied or withdrawn'; attention values are the live substates of open. Satisfied and withdrawn are rest. A record coming to rest moves waiting to ready; a new filing starts at ready.

session-2026-09-16-schema-close.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim: "It might be a no-op in the sense that the steward wakes up, sees, 'Oh, this record is done, but that's okay because everything else has already been filed,' so it moves it back. It's an unnecessary wake, but it requires judgment anyway, so that's fine." "question 10, I'm fine with your recommendation. Let's try to copy the same patterns we've already established." "I'm fine with what you said there: intentions as a type of record." (i.e. agreed with the recommendation that an intention is not a record)

reassessment-reason-on-event.text: Each reassessment appends one event to the intention's log carrying the steward's choice (more work, wait, send to desk, settle) and its reason as the payload, the same pattern as the dials trace on the send-to-desk event. There is no second place for the steward's reasoning.

intention-is-not-a-record.text: An intention is not a record. It reuses the record's machinery (event log, one state dimension with rest states) but not its governance: no contract, no store, no orchestrator claim, no artifacts. Making it a record would put it inside the frame it sits above.

session-2026-09-16-claimability-not-waki.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim: "the problem I have is 'wakes'. It's a thing that is claimable, so the agent may or may not be running. That's up to the user, right? Whether they're currently running that agent type or not." "We don't have the machinery for waking an orchestrator necessarily ... I don't necessarily want to build that yet." claimability-not-waking.text: The kernel records claimability, never wakes anyone. Birth makes an item claimable by its claimer (a new record by the orchestrator, a new flag by the auditor). Rest of a rung makes the rung above claimable again. Resolution of a block makes the held rung claimable again (an auditor's ruling makes the record claimable by the orchestrator under the changed contract; no worker is woken). Whether an agent is running to claim is running policy, not the model.

observations-wait-for-inbox-run.text: Filing an agent-filed intention does not make the steward's inbox ready. Agent-filed intentions sit until the user runs the inbox under the recency dials; only then are they claimable by the steward.

intention-kind-is-origin.text: An intention's kind is its filing origin, with two shipped values: person-filed (the operator or anyone outside) and agent-filed (an agent in the course of its work; the observation). Kind is the running policy's routing key to an inbox. Subject (bug, feature, question) is never a field: the steward decides what a filing is by reading it, and may find that a claimed bug is not one and settle the intention. Subtypes may be added under the two values later.

one-actor-one-item-kind-v3.text: Each actor claims exactly one kind of item and no other: the steward claims intentions, the orchestrator claims records, the worker claims runs, the auditor claims flags, the operator claims desk items. The contract writer claims nothing; contract changes are frame work. Any actor's judgment may birth items of another kind, but claiming is exclusive. An intention can birth many records and many desk items.

intention-state-transitions.text: Transitions of the four-value state, each caused by one operation or event. ready: on file-intention, or on record rest while waiting, or when a desk item on it is answered while waiting. claimed: when the steward begins reassess-intention. waiting: when reassess chooses more work (records created) or wait, or sends the intention to the desk. settled: on settle-intention, by the steward or the operator, with satisfied or withdrawn as the event payload; final. mockups-are-a-store.text: Mockups, design packets and other proposals are records in a store a user may define, produced by a worker at a node. The steward never makes one and no built-in actor is a designer; the steward files the first record and reads the rest, and the desk shows the proposal through the linked record.

desk-shows-operator-seats.text: The desk lists everything the operator owes the next action on, from two sources: items sent up by the steward or the orchestrator, and records resting at a node whose seat is the operator (judgment human, host operator). A record at an operator seat is projected onto the desk by the kernel as a desk item; the operator's answer there is any legal act at that seat (walk, enrich, patch, archive), and the item is answered when the record leaves the seat. The operator still claims only desk items.

desk-card-is-words.text: A desk item's card is words from its sender. Any options on it are the sender's own statement of its legal next moves, in those words, unenforced by the kernel. The operator's answer is words: a pick, free text, or a rework instruction (redo, refresh, reword). The sender reads the answer and acts, and sends again if it must; redo, refresh and rework are answers, not desk verbs.

desk-item-answered-once.text: A desk item is answered exactly once and is then closed; its state has two values, open and answered. A further round (a new mockup, the rest of a partial answer) is a new desk item that links the previous one. The sender must act between answers, so each round is a new send.

desk-renders-from-affordances.text: The desk renders an operator seat mechanically from the kernel's typed legal affordances: each outgoing edge is a button, an edge with only optional payload is a button plus a notes box, an edge with required fields is a form, an enum field is one button per value, archive is always present. No contract-specific UI. Authoring guidance: keep an operator seat to edges with optional payloads; the compiler warns when an operator seat has a required non-enum field.

desk-item-schema-draft.text: Schema of a desk item. Origin: id, sender (steward, orchestrator, or none when the kernel projects a record at an operator seat), the card text in the sender's words including any options, the sender's trace (dials weighed, the orchestrator's reason, or the seat's legal affordances). Links: one or more intentions; zero or more records; the subset of those records frozen while open; the previous desk item when this is a new round. One state: open, answered; answered is final. History: one append-only log on the kernel's event machinery: sent, discussion entries by the operator or a co-seat, acts at a seat (enrich, patch), answered (the answer text or the leaving act as payload, with actor). No artifacts of its own; a proposal is a linked record's artifact. Mirrored into the sender's thread; an answer in either place is the one answer.

pen-is-the-claim.text: The steward claims an intention the way the orchestrator claims a record: by taking the kernel's pen, process-anchored, one pen per place (C16). intention-single-state-v4.text: An intention has one state with three values: ready, waiting, settled. Settled is the one rest state, final; the outcome, satisfied or withdrawn, is the payload of the settle event. There is no claimed value: the steward's claim is the kernel's pen. A person-filed intention starts at ready. An agent-filed intention starts at waiting until an inbox run moves it to ready. A direct add's intention starts at waiting because an attempt is already in flight. A record coming to rest moves waiting to ready.

intention-state-transitions-v3.text: Transitions of the three-value state. ready: on file-intention by a person, on an inbox run reaching an agent-filed intention, on record rest while waiting, or when a desk item linked to it is answered while waiting. waiting: on file-intention by an agent, on a direct add, or when reassess chooses more work or wait or sends the intention to the desk. settled: on settle-intention by the steward or the operator, satisfied or withdrawn as payload; final. Merge and discard by the steward are settle withdrawn with a reason naming the surviving intention. No other transitions exist.

direct-add-rest-rule.text: An agent-filed intention that already has a record (an agent's direct add) follows the rest rule: when its record rests the intention becomes ready. The inbox rule applies only to agent-filed intentions with no record.

intention-kind-derived-from-session.text: An intention's kind is derived at filing: no agent session on the command means person-filed, an agent session means agent-filed; a human who ran become is acting as that agent. An explicit --kind overrides either way.

no-intention-backfill.text: Records that exist before the direct add door lands get no backfilled intention. The rule that every record is an attempt at an intention holds for records created from that door onward; only active triage records are drained into intentions at migration.

desk-answer-readies-all-linked.text: When a desk item is answered, every intention linked to it that is waiting becomes ready. The steward re-reads each and may put some straight back to waiting.

delegates-are-co-seats-v2.text: The assistant and the architect are not actors. They are the operator with a co-seat on one of the operator's own desk items: the assistant on a desk item for hours, the architect on a long-lived desk item that the steward sent up for an intention the dials route to the desk, for weeks. The operator never claims an intention. A design session is the operator working one such desk item with a co-seat; the theory graph is that seat's ledger. Any user-defined agent has three coordinates: which operator item it shares, how it is driven, how long it lives.

seat-act-is-one-transaction.text: At an operator seat the desk submits a button press with its payload as one transaction: enrich then walk; if the walk is refused the enrich is rolled back.

auditor-may-send-to-desk.text: The auditor is a desk sender alongside the steward and the orchestrator, because its resolver is the operator.

team-ruling-is-desk-item.text: A ruling needed by a team construct is an execution question: a desk item sent by the orchestrator, not a flag. No change is made until teams are live (D310).

stand-in-and-repair-without-flags.text: Constitution C11 and C17 stop using the word flag. An orchestrator stand-in after silence on blocked work is an entry on the still-open desk item, which stays open until the operator answers. A brief repair under C17 is recorded as an agent-filed intention. The constitution wording is the operator's edit.

ruling-release-gates-claimability.text: After an auditor ruling that changed the contract, the held record becomes claimable once the new release is applied to it. After a ruling that changed nothing, it is claimable at once. Release promotion itself is left as is.

frozen-record-still-judged.text: While a flag holds a record, the orchestrator may still judge the record side of a combined block and record its disposition: hand back, archive, or ask the operator. Only starting a new run waits for both blocks to resolve.

first-build-leaves-three-things.text: The first build leaves three things as they are: the prepared-packet decision route (the tasks and ideas stores' operator seats depend on it), the materialize adapter (dormant until directions retire into intentions), and the become types demo, trial concierge and other; assistant folds into the co-seat. Retired triage records are archived with one reason.

memory-cells-stay.text: The memory cells under .mor/mem/<distro>/<role>.json stay exactly as they are: not deleted, not re-keyed, not modified by this build. They are the orchestrator's and the other roles' standing (S-band) and transient (T-band) memory at the distro, and they answer half one of the memory problem: what survives a context wipe for the same role is its memory cell plus the items it holds and their logs. There is no private memory in the sense of hidden state; a cell is the memory at the role's place, per C16.

code-check-2026-09-17-role-identity.text: Assistant's reading of the code on main, 2026-09-17, not Blake's words. (1) agent_sessions has uniqueness indexes per process anchor, per harness key, per explicit token and per record, and none per role (crates/mor-kernel/src/agent_session/mod.rs, index block). (2) The only one-orchestrator guard is an advisory lease file .mor/mem/<distro>/orchestrator.session-lease written by packaging/npm/morphisms/lib/orchestrator.js updateSessionLease; it warns when the recorded pid is alive and starts anyway, and runs only on the morphisms orchestrator launcher path. (3) The live orchestrator session row is identified_by harness_env (Claude Code) and holds no record; worker rows hold the record pens and are resolved by the runner's correlation. (4) A key-identified session is live for thirty minutes after last_seen; a process-anchored session is live while its process is (session_is_live_at). (5) The intention pen refuses harness_env and explicit_token sessions (crates/mor-kernel/src/intention.rs pen_session) although every session row records an anchor pid and start token. (6) Claude Code, Pi and Codex export their session key into every shell, so become inside a harness is always key-identified; bounded record B1788 (E1) showed a launched steward refused with pen_requires_process_session (triage record TRI1826) and ships a persona workaround that unsets the key before become.

role-exclusion-advisory-until-design.text: Until the design session on process identity and the pen on a role, exclusion of the steward and of the orchestrator is advisory: being unable to enforce one holder per role is a shortcoming to record, not a defect that returns work.

process-identity-and-role-pen.text: How does the kernel know which running process holds a role, and is one holder per role per distro enforced by a kernel pen or left to running policy? The design says the pen is process-anchored and that one steward and one orchestrator per distro is removed by configuration, not by state. The build found that become records the harness conversation key instead of the process whenever a harness key is present, that the pen refuses such sessions, and that nothing in the kernel limits a role to one holder.

what-does-the-orchestrator-hold.text: What does the orchestrator hold a pen on, and how does the kernel know which process is the orchestrator? The design says the orchestrator claims records the way the steward claims an intention. Blake says the orchestrator holds the pen for spawning workers and creating runs. In the build the orchestrator session holds no record; workers hold the record pens and the runner anchors them with no owner. One orchestrator per distro is kept only by advisory lock files; the kernel limits no role to one holder, and become records the harness conversation key instead of the process whenever a harness key is present.

intention-source-and-context-slot.text: Does an intention carry a field for where it came from and the context it was filed with? The schema has one text slot. In the build every front door that adds context writes it into the text: the triage drain writes the source record id as a trailing line, and the Workbench form writes a marker line that its retry check and the My requests list read back.

retired-store-read-lifetime.text: How long must the archived rows of a retired store be kept, and what may a read of a retired store cost? In the build a store the current release no longer declares stays readable only while some row, archived rows included, still pins a release that declares it, so those rows can never be hard-deleted, and each such read loads every distinct pinned release (reported as 34 releases of about 2.5 MB on the live database, not measured).

landed-knowledge-reaches-dependent-brief.text: When a record's wait on another record settles, how does what the predecessor actually built reach the dependent record's brief before it is checked? In the build a brief written before its predecessor merged was stale at the merge on A2, B1, C1b, E1 (three times) and F1b; the brief check caught each at the cost of one repair round, and the knowledge was carried by hand.

seat-model-unavailable-hold.text: How does a seat say that the model its work is routed to is unavailable, so the record holds there visibly? Blake's rule is hold, never substitute a model for a quota problem. In the build the store could not see quota, records sat with dead workers until a human-shaped ruling arrived, and the orchestrator shared one quota with the workers it watches. Related: the roster routes by seat and cannot route by kind of record.

direct-add-intention-text-fallback.text: On a direct add, where does the intention's text come from when the caller gives none? The build first refused the add, which broke every fixture contract and old caller and turned main red; a stand-in then ruled the text optional: the flag, else the store's declared summary field, else the record id. Blake has not ratified or reversed that.

desk-freeze-has-no-effect.text: What may freeze a record, and through which check? The design lets a desk item freeze records while it is open. In the build the desk writes the frozen link and nothing reads it: the check for whether the source item is open knows intentions only, the flags task adds flags to it, and desk items stay out, so a record frozen by a desk item remains claimable.

direct-add-kind-is-always-agent.text: Should the operator's own direct add be labelled person-filed? The design derives kind from the session: no agent session means person-filed. In the build direct add refuses any caller without a session, so every direct add is agent-filed, the operator's included; only a tooling caller yields person.

reassess-guard-is-up-front.text: Is reassess still one guarded append? In the build the expected sequence is checked first, the effects run and append their own events, and the reassessed event is then appended at the current sequence without a second guard, all in one transaction.

bulk-filing-floods-the-steward.text: When many person-filed intentions are filed at once, what stops a running steward from seeing them all as ready at the same moment? A person-filed intention is ready at birth. The triage drain will file one per open triage record, 127 on the live database on 17 Sep. The inbox dials bound agent-filed intentions only. Options named so far: run the drain with the steward stopped, or file the drained intentions so they wait behind the inbox dials.

release-gate-is-same-not-later.text: Is a record held by a flag ruling until a later release, or until exactly the gate release? The design says later. The flags task as planned says the record's release must equal the gate release, because the kernel has no order over release ids.

thread-answer-clears-both.text: Does answering or dismissing a question in the agent thread always clear it from the desk too? The design says the answer clears it from both. The thread mirror as planned: the kernel commits first and the thread mirrors it; a dismissed or deferred question keeps its desk item open until answered at the terminal; and a question reaches the desk only if the orchestrator's holds carry its name, which the steward and orchestrator task leaves empty.

code-check-2026-09-18-steward-launch-pat.text: Assistant's reading of the code on main, 2026-09-18, not Blake's words. Two launch paths exist. (1) Operator-started roles go through launchAgent in packaging/npm/morphisms/lib/agent-host.js: a full harness session (pi or claude) that runs mor become <role> itself; no roster route, no hydrate, no pen reserved for it. morphisms orchestrator start, contract_writer and every mor become role use it. (2) System-started workers go through morphisms worker spawn and workers/runner.mjs: roster-routed per node (model, harness, effort), one hydrate holding one record or a declared batch of records, the pen reserved on the record before launch, blocks until the worker exits. The steward is a third shape: packaging/npm/morphisms/lib/steward.js is a sense loop (every 30 s, mor intention ls --claimable) that, when something is claimable and no session it launched is alive, launches ONE session through path (1) with role steward. That session claims one intention, reassesses once, releases, exits; release also ends its session row (ledger GAP-19). orchestrator start under orchestrator_auto_spawn runs the same loop shape. No roster entry, model or batch size exists for the steward; agents.js holds only steward always_on|on_demand, orchestrator_auto_spawn and inbox_kinds.

orchestrator-as-the-one-launcher.text: Should the orchestrator be the one launcher of every system-started agent, the steward included, so that the steward runs as a roster-routed session (model, harness, effort, batch size) over a batch of claimable intentions the way a worker runs over a batch of records? Today the steward is a third shape: its own sense loop launches one operator-style become session per claimable intention, with no roster route and no batch. Operator-started agents (orchestrator, contract writer, auditor, demo, concierge) are the first kind; orchestrator-spawned workers are the second; the steward fits neither. Open sub-questions: whether the steward would then sit below the orchestrator on the ladder rather than above it (attempt-ladder), and whether the orchestrator spawning the steward breaks or respects one-actor-one-item-kind-v3 (spawning is not claiming).

session-2026-09-18-desk-sections.text: Blake, 2026-09-18, in chat, verbatim excerpts. On options: "Desk card options are text or schema; they absolutely must be schema. I don't know why anyone would think interpreting freeform markdown is a good idea at all." "Every steward filing on a desk item must come with built-in options. The orchestrator can also file to my desk, and they'll always have to give options. When I return an item with one of those options, they can act on it." On the desk: "The desk is basically anything I should see." "My desk should have different compartments, like a physical desk with drawers. There's the raw inbox, which comes from the steward ... I can stamp it and put it in the outbox." "Instead of putting them back in the inbox, I want another slot, a drawer, a category, a section of my desk, specifically for 'I need to talk to my colleague about this.'" "Those agents aren't really separate; they're co-pens or co-seats with me, tools I use. The desk item isn't moved off my desk; it stays on my desk but in a different compartment." "Just like I currently press D for discuss and A for architect. We'll keep that, but it will be an internal desk configuration: a setting that lets me map keyboard shortcuts to sections." "I might even have a mockup section." "What is canonical and what is configurable? ... I don't know yet, but we'll start with the ability to define different sections of the desk." On the explain card: "The explain card was designed to help me understand something after the fact, but I want it to provide more context up front ... 'What is this?' Then a second field, longer, expands on the first; a third field, even longer ... Not a different language, just more detail. 'What is this? Why is this? How will this be done (or how was this done)?'" "I don't think you can apply the schema right now, but this needs to be built later." On the brief: "In general, the steward should not be filing the brief, but right now it's a design flaw in the bounded dimension, the bounded store, so that's to be fixed." "I'm going to do a distro-wide contract upgrade." On routing: "Each store has documentation, just like edges have documentation ... every store will have a documented purpose." desk-card-options-are-schema.text: A desk item's options are a schema field on the item, never prose a surface parses. Every send to the desk, by the steward, the orchestrator or the auditor, carries its options, and a send without them is refused at filing time. The operator's answer is one option plus optional words, and the sender acts on the returned option. The live triage packet's choices field (id, label, consequence, act) and its decision enum (numbered picks, discuss, architect, hold, close, redo) are the prior art to reuse, not reinvent.

desk-has-sections.text: The desk is one list with sections, like drawers in a physical desk. Two are canonical: the inbox, where every send arrives, and the outbox, where answered items go. The operator may define further sections for items kept open but not answerable cold: discuss, architect, mockup. Moving an item to a section is not answering it; the item stays open on the desk and its sender keeps waiting. Desk configuration maps a keyboard shortcut to each section, so today's D for discuss and A for architect become two entries in that map. Which sections beyond inbox and outbox are system-owned is not yet decided.

meta.title: section agent is a co seat

section-agent-is-a-co-seat.text: A user-defined desk section may name one agent that works only with the operator on the items in that section: the assistant on the discuss section, the architect on the architect section, a mockup maker on the mockup section. That agent is the operator's co-seat, a tool the operator runs, never an actor of its own; the operator starts it, and the item never leaves the desk while they work.

explanation-is-three-tiers.text: Every desk item carries a schema-enforced explanation in three fields of increasing length and the same plain language: what this is, why it is here, and how it will be done or how it was done. The sender fills all three up front, when it sends; a send without them is refused. This replaces the explain card, which was written after the fact to explain a decision already taken. Not built yet; the schema is the first build step.

desk-item-schema-v2.text: Schema of a desk item, second draft. Origin: id, sender (steward, orchestrator, auditor, or none when the kernel projects a record at an operator seat), the sender's trace. Content, all schema-enforced at send: the explanation in three tiers (what, why, how), the options (id, label, consequence, act), and the sender's recommendation if it has one. Place: the section the item sits in, inbox on arrival. Links, state, history and mirroring are unchanged from the first draft: linked intentions and records, held subset, previous item; one state open or answered, answered final; one append-only log; mirrored into the sender's thread.

steward-does-not-brief.text: The steward never writes a brief. That a record the steward files cannot route until someone attaches a brief and submits it is a design flaw in the bounded store's contract, written for a world without a steward. Neither a third briefing seat nor a steward that briefs is the fix; the fix is a distro-wide contract redesign in which the brief is produced by a store whose declared output is a good brief.

stores-carry-documentation.text: Each store in a contract may declare documentation of itself, as edges do today: its purpose, what kind of item enters it, and what kind of output leaves it. Example: input, an uncertain bug report that may or may not still be active; output, an investigation report that says whether it is. The declaration is optional, so no existing contract breaks.

steward-routes-by-store-documentation.text: The steward's packet carries a bird's-eye view of every store's documentation. When it chooses more work it picks the store whose declared input matches the item, and when that store's output comes back it reads it against the declared output to choose the next store or settle. Example: an uncertain bug report goes to a bug-investigation store; a report saying no bug settles the intention; a report saying a wide bug goes to a brief-planning store, a reshaping of today's observation store; a good brief goes to the bounded store.

desk-sections-canonical-vs-configurable.text: Beyond the inbox and the outbox, which desk sections, shortcuts and section agents are system-owned and which are the operator's own configuration? Blake on 2026-09-18: not decided; start with the ability to define sections. Also open: whether the two canonical marks (make this a rule, this should not have come to me) stay marks beside the answer, become options on every card, or become sections.

bounded-store-redesign-with-steward.text: How does the bounded store change now that the steward creates every record and never briefs? Where is the brief written: in a brief-planning store that reshapes the observation store, whose output is a good brief? Do intake and brief_repair survive, or does their check move to the brief-planning store's terminal? What does the steward's more-work act carry when it files into a store that expects a brief? When a record's wait on another record settles, how does what the predecessor actually built reach the dependent brief before it is checked? In the build such briefs were stale at the merge on A2, B1, C1b, E1 (three times) and F1b, each costing one repair round, the knowledge carried by hand. This is the distro-wide contract upgrade Blake named on 2026-09-18; it is its own design session.

store-documentation-dsl-shape.text: What does a store's documentation block look like in the .mor DSL (purpose, input, output; free text or typed against the store's artifact kinds), and how does it reach the steward's packet: a compiled view over every store in the release, or the agent manual? Related: the steward packet is already 27 KB, half of it the distro manual.

session-2026-09-18-sections-option-one.text: Blake, 2026-09-18, verbatim: "Let's lock in option one." Option one as put to him: sections are desk configuration, in the kernel as one field. A desk item gets a section column; a move is one command and the item stays open. The list of sections, each with its shortcut and the agent role that serves it, lives in one config file next to the dials. Inbox is no section yet and outbox is answered, so both fall out of state. Every named section is the operator's own. The agent for a section is a role the operator starts by hand. Nothing touches the contract. The two canonical marks stay marks. Rejected: sections as contract states (the retiring triage pattern), and Workbench-only tags (agents could not see them).

desk-sections-are-desk-configuration.text: A desk item carries one section field in the kernel. A move sets it in one act and the item stays open; moving is not answering. Inbox is an item with no section and outbox is an answered item, so both derive from state and neither is configured. Every named section, its keyboard shortcut and the role that serves it are declared in one desk configuration file beside the dials, and the kernel refuses a move to a section that file does not name. A section's role is started by the operator and reads the items in its section. No contract change; the triage store's discuss and architect states are the old pattern and retire with it. The two canonical marks stay marks.

desk-item-may-hold-records.text: There is one hold mechanism. A record is claimable when no open item rests on it, and three kinds of item can rest on a record: an intention, while unsettled; a flag, on the records the auditor names; a desk item, on the records the sender names at send, optionally. The hold releases when the item closes; for a desk item that is its answer. after.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "The terminal node in one of the dimensions of a store does not necessarily always mean that the work was completed successfully. ... it means that the movement of this record through this dimension has come to rest." "what completed means is that there is no more movement of this thing through that dimension." "the steward should be woken if the record has completed, or in this case, if the record has been abandoned. I don't know what our schema choice is here; this is an open question." "the steward waking conditions are on a new intention that has been filed and not processed." "The operator will not be the handover mechanism from the orchestrator to the steward. Instead, there should be some kind of artifact or reference note, probably written by the orchestrator, that will explain what went wrong, why, and what the orchestrator's recommendation is. Ultimately, it's up to the steward what to do." "Maybe the archive has a note, and that note is the handover from orchestrator to steward."

A terminal state in a dimension means the record's movement through that dimension has come to rest, not that the work succeeded. An investigation that finds no problem ends at rest. A record archived before reaching a terminal state has also come to rest.

meta.title: Terminal means rest, not success

after.text: Two shapes cover everything that happens to an intention on the ladder: it moves (an attempt: record, run) or it is blocked (an obstruction: a desk item, or a flag when the contract is the cause). Obstructions go sideways, are born from the blocked claimer, are claimed by a resolver, rest when answered, and wake the raiser. An observation is neither: it is a new intention entering the front door.

before.text: Two shapes cover everything that happens to an intention on the ladder: it moves (an attempt: record, run) or it is blocked (an obstruction: a desk item, or a flag when the contract is the cause). Attempts go down the ladder, are born from the claimer above, are claimed by a doer, rest when the walk ends, and wake the claimer above. Obstructions go sideways, are born from the blocked claimer, are claimed by a resolver, rest when answered, and wake the raiser. An observation is neither: it is a new intention entering the front door.

The steward never writes a brief. That a record the steward files cannot route until someone attaches a brief and submits it is a design flaw in the bounded store's contract, written for a world without a steward. Neither a third briefing seat nor a steward that briefs is the fix; the fix is a distro-wide contract redesign in which the brief is produced by a store whose declared output is a good brief.

Each store in a contract may declare documentation of itself, as edges do today: its purpose, what kind of item enters it, and what kind of output leaves it. Example: input, an uncertain bug report that may or may not still be active; output, an investigation report that says whether it is. The declaration is optional, so no existing contract breaks.

The steward's packet carries a bird's-eye view of every store's documentation. When it chooses more work it picks the store whose declared input matches the item, and when that store's output comes back it reads it against the declared output to choose the next store or settle. Example: an uncertain bug report goes to a bug-investigation store; a report saying no bug settles the intention; a report saying a wide bug goes to a brief-planning store, a reshaping of today's observation store; a good brief goes to the bounded store.

after.text: Blake, 2026-09-18, verbatim excerpts: "I don't like the idea of creating a freeze because there's already a hold mechanism ... We don't need another notion of putting a hold on something." "I think it should be optional ... if something gets filed to the desk, then the agent filing it has authority to put a hold on it. That's all." "Whoever files a desk item should determine if it's linked to a record or an intention. It will intrinsically be linked to an intention, but also, if it's explicitly linked to a record ... put a hold on some record and link that hold to the desk item so that once the desk item has been processed, the hold can be triggered to recognize that the holding condition has been satisfied." "This is the same as the dependency situation we have on records, where we can file an explicit depends on field." On the assistant's reading (one mechanism, three items that rest on a record, released when the item closes; the sender names records, the intention waits automatically; his word hold wins where he reads): "yes, I think this is fine. record this in the graph." And: "if IN3 is a few lines, use opus subagent to fix this now directly."

There is one hold mechanism. A record is claimable when no open item rests on it, and three kinds of item can rest on a record: an intention, while unsettled; a flag, on the records the auditor names; a desk item, on the records the sender names at send, optionally. The hold releases when the item closes; for a desk item that is its answer. A desk item always links at least one intention, and that intention waits automatically until the item is answered; the hold on records never cascades from the intention, the sender chooses each record with judgment. This is the same shape as a record waiting on another record, with a different release condition. Where the operator reads it the word is hold, never freeze; the kernel's internal name for the link may stay until that code is touched. Which section of the desk the item sits in has no bearing on the hold.

after.text: Assistant's reading of the code on main, 2026-09-18, by a read-only agent; not Blake's words. (1) The worker runner reserves record pens before launch with 'mor agent session reserve --store --record (xN) --node --role --correlation' (workers/pi-extension/core-v3.mjs:747-799). The reserved row has no holder: anchor pid NULL, identity carried by the correlation (agent_session/mod.rs:4056-4085). The launched worker exports its anchor pid and the correlation, and its first command, hydrate, adopts the row: lifecycle reserved to live with the anchor set (mod.rs:4646-4700). A batch is repeated --record under one savepoint; one held member refuses the whole batch. (2) 'mor intention claim' is strictly self-service: it inserts a live row for the calling process and refuses a session identified by a harness key, because such a session lives by an idle window and could hold a pen forever (intention.rs:897-909, 349-352). No reserve verb exists for an intention pen. (3) Intention pens and record pens share one table, agent_sessions; a pen row is store 'intention', record the IN id, dimension_state 'intention.pen' (intention.rs:129-135). 'agent session reserve' does not check that the record is a real record, so it would accept an IN id today. (4) The roster file .mor/worker-roster.json is keyed '<store>/<dimension.state>' with harness, model, effort, account per key over a default; the steward has no entry, only running_policy (always_on or on_demand, inbox_kinds) read by steward.js. (5) After exit the runner settles the pen row by correlation and anchor, which is not record-shaped; the verdict on the work (accepted_walk, multi_walk, none_observed) reads record events and edge keys and is wholly record-shaped (runner.mjs:632-835, work-order.mjs:125-200). (6) 'mor become steward' returns role instructions only; there is no 'mor intention hydrate'. 'mor flag hydrate' is a precedent for hydrating an item. (7) The worker spawn flag for a collaborative seat only widens spawn admission; the launch stays headless with no agent thread. (8) 'A steward is running' is known only to the npm launcher: <workspace>/.mor/<distro>-steward.lock and a status file beside it (steward.js:31-137). Neither the kernel nor the Workbench reads them.
